newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW- Banacci bad loan woes persist.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW- Banacci bad loan woes persist.

text.p: Banamex-Accival (Banacci), Mexico's largest banking group, makes no apologies for shocking investors last week by unveiling larger-than-expected projections for its first-quarter past-due loan performance.
"You can either break bad news gradually or break it all at once. We did it in one go, " Jorge Hierro, deputy director general of Banacci, said in an interview on Thursday.

Investors had been led to believe that past-due loans would double under new international bank accounting rules introduced in Mexico on January 1. So they were stunned last week to discover from Banacci's numbers that the problem was far worse than that.

Under the U.S. GAAP rules, past-due loans at Banamex, Banacci's banking unit, would have grown by about 150 percent if Banacci had not sold off an eight million peso bundle of loans, net of reserves, to the government in late December.
Moreover, Hierro indicated on Thursday that as far as unpaid loans go, Banamex is not quite out of the woods yet.

Though the situation has improved since 1995, when Mexico's banking crisis peaked, in the latter half of 1996 past-due loans continued to grow quarter-on-quarter in single digits. That general growth rate is expected to persist for a while.
"It's very difficult to say we've hit bottom. We're close," he said. "We expect (past-due loan growth) will continue in single digits in the coming quarters, on a downward trend."

That growth was likely to come chiefly from commercial and mortgage clients, he said. There were also some lingering problems -- that he stressed were "not generalized" -- with debtors with restructured loans who are in default again.

Hierro denied there was any deliberate attempt to mislead the markets when Banacci estimated late last year -- as did the National Banking and Securities Commission -- that past-due loans would at most double under U.S. GAAP rules.
He said that was the bank's "best estimate" at the time, based on the preliminary version of the GAAP rules.
Also, the past-due loan situation among mortgage and commercial debtors in the fourth quarter "did not improve as fast as we had expected," he said.
A rebound in interest rates at the end of last year plagued some commercial and mortgage debtors. A slide in the peso also hurt some clients with dollar loans, he said.

Based on the new GAAP rules, Banacci estimated that in the first quarter, past-due loans, net of the eight million it sold to the bank insurance fund Fobaproa, would surge to 21.316 billion pesos, from 10.624 billion pesos at the end of 1996.

Part of that calculation, Hierro said, was based on an assessment of current loans whose payments were behind schedule in December and that were likely to be officially in default by the end of March.

Since it released its report, Banacci's share price has swooned. On Thursday its B shares stood at 15.36 pesos, down from a high of 17.30 pesos at the close on January 15. Still, Hierro's perception of analysts' reaction to last week's news was "neutral to good."
He acknowledged that there was a lingering problem with net interest margins, which shrank in the fourth quarter and may continue to do so going forward.

Hierro estimated that the effect of the new GAAP rules on interest income would cut another 100 basis points off its margin. He said growing competition in the Mexican banking market was likely to take a further toll.

He also noted that the bank has more low-risk, low-return government paper among its assets. It received the paper in exchange for selling loans to Fobaproa last year, which also puts a lid on interest income.

On the other hand, he said, with reserves under U.S. GAAP at an estimated 60 percent of past-due loans, 15 percentage points more than the minimum required by law, the bank would have less need to provision in the future.
That, he added, will contribute to protecting what he describes as his main concern -- the bottom line. "We hope to have reasonable profits in the first quarter," he said.
((-- Mexico City newsroom +525 728-9560))
